summary.text: A 69-year-old man with hypertension, previously hospitalized in intensive care for severe COVID-19 with bronchopneumonia and respiratory failure and treated with favipiravir, dexamethasone, anticoagulant, antibiotics and CPAP, was discharged after 14 days dependent on a mobile oxygen device. In the third month after the hospitalization he presented to the Infectious Diseases Daily Clinic with severe stomatitis of the gums and palate, asthenia and difficulty eating, and a 2-week fluconazole course gave no clinical response.

Three days after discharge he had Clostridium difficile diarrhea treated with oral rehydration and oral vancomycin, and on Day-28 left hemiparesis, left eyeball symptoms and unilateral visual loss appeared, with left eye examination and ophthalmoscopy findings. A post-COVID stroke was diagnosed in the ambulatory setting, brain imaging was scheduled and the patient chose home care. Oral cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and later Candida species, and necrotic oral lesions spread to the left hemipalate.

Head MRI showed pansinusitis, left sinus obliteration, an ischemic-character left cortical image and a fluid image suggesting a nasogenian abscess. Biopsy of necrotic left hemi-palate tissue showed non-septate hyphae with the appearance of mucormycosis and no neoplastic cells, and rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis related to COVID-19 was diagnosed; diabetes was excluded and bacterial and Candida superinfections were confirmed.

Treatment combined piperacillin/tazobactam for 21 days, oral posaconazole for a six-month course (the first-line amphotericin was not available), and step-by-step excisions until complete removal of necrotic tissue, which left the left hemi-palate lost with a large oro-antral communication on CT. Neurological dysfunction improved in six months and laboratory markers improved, but left eye blindness was irreversible; after 9 months from COVID-19 the palate was reconstructed with a dental prosthesis, restoring mastication.
